decks.name: Worn transport

decks.help: Worn, filthy, and still in use.
decks.name: Neglected

parameters.help: Antenna signal level. Lowering it brings snow first, then flickering and lost color as the color burst drowns, then broken sync as the sync pulses do — the order a real set fails in.
parameters.label: Signal strength

parameters.help: The vertical oscillator's free-running speed. Near the center the sync pulses pull it into lock; past the lock range the picture rolls, with the blanking bar crossing the screen.
parameters.label: Vertical hold

parameters.help: The horizontal oscillator's free-running speed. Off center the picture slides sideways as the AFC strains to hold it; further and lock breaks — the picture tears into diagonal bands and the color goes wild.
parameters.label: Horizontal hold

parameters.help: How quickly the TV's horizontal AFC follows timing changes. Slow sets ride out noise but bend at the top of the picture on VCR playback (flagging); fast ones track tape timing but jitter in noise.
parameters.label: AFC response

parameters.help: Raises the picture tube's black level, as turning up a TV's brightness did. The blanking intervals and sync pulses become visible when the picture rolls or tears.
parameters.label: Brightness

parameters.help: A reflected copy of the signal arriving late (multipath). Negative values invert it, as reflections often did. Its color shifts with the delay, because the delayed color carrier arrives at a different phase.
parameters.label: Ghost

parameters.help: How late the reflection arrives. 1 µs is about 2% of the picture width — a reflection path roughly 300 m longer than the direct one.
parameters.label: Ghost delay

parameters.help: Mains hum leaking into the video: light and dark bars that drift slowly up the picture (60 Hz hum against the 59.94 Hz color field rate), bending the picture where the sync separator is pulled off.
parameters.label: Hum

parameters.help: Line 21 carries closed-caption data — the row of dashes visible in the blanking bar when the picture rolls.
parameters.label: Caption data

parameters.help: Which cassette: another one in the same condition, with its own flaws in their own places, its tracks bent a little differently and its sticky patches elsewhere. On a clean tape there's nothing to move, so it looks the same.
parameters.label: Cassette

parameters.help: The tape speed it was recorded at. LP and EP move the tape on half or a third as far between fields, so the tracks are narrower and closer: a slightly noisier picture, color crosstalk from the neighboring tracks that the deck's comb filter has to cancel, flaws that take longer to pass (a damaged stretch of tape plays for three times as long in EP), and less forgiveness of tracking errors and skew.
parameters.label: Recorded at

parameters.help: How many times the picture was dubbed from tape to tape before this one, at this tape's speed. Each copy is really played back, sent over a composite cable — where the recording deck has to pull picture and color apart again, losing fine detail and mistaking some of it for color — and recorded again: softness, noise, smeared color and every deck's timing errors pile up.
parameters.label: Generation

parameters.help: Age and plays. The magnetic coating weakens and roughens, so the heads read a weaker signal over a slightly larger gap — noisier pictures, then sparkles where the signal sinks to the FM threshold — and pinholes appear in the oxide.
parameters.label: Wear

parameters.help: Pinholes and flakes missing from the magnetic coating: dropouts. Each is a short dash that starts with a spark, somewhere new every field; turn it up for more of them, a blizzard at the top. With Dropout compensation on the deck fills each dash from the line above; off, they are black and white streaks and they jog the picture. A flaw smaller than one 58 µm track only weakens the signal, and is seen only when the signal is weak already.
parameters.label: Oxide flaws

parameters.help: Scratches along the tape from worn guides. Height across the tape is height in the picture, so a lengthwise scratch is a thin sparkling line right across, at the same height in every field. Turn it up for more lines, not thicker ones.
parameters.label: Scratches

parameters.help: Folds across the tape. The heads cross each one a little earlier every field, so it sweeps up through the picture as a band of noise over a few seconds; the fold also shortens the track, a timing jump the TV has to chase.
parameters.label: Creases

parameters.help: Crinkled tape edges, from a deck that chewed it. The tracks start at the bottom edge and end at the top, so the damage lifts the tape off the heads at the top and bottom of the picture.
parameters.label: Edge damage

parameters.help: Fungus colonies, thickest near the edges where it grows in the wound pack. Each one lifts the tape off the heads and eats into the coating, and it sheds — what it sheds collects on the heads.
parameters.label: Mold

parameters.help: The binder holding the oxide on has soaked up moisture and gone gummy in patches. The tape plays clean until a patch reaches the guides; then it sticks — edges shiver as it squeals, the top of the picture leans and noise creeps in as the tape drags — and tears loose with a sideways lurch. Turn it up for patches that come more often and hold harder. The gummy oxide also clogs the heads.
parameters.label: Sticky shed

parameters.help: A film smeared on the tape, holding the heads off it. Spacing costs the short-wavelength picture signal far more than the long-wavelength color, so the picture breaks into noise while color survives and smears. It rubs off onto the heads, too.
parameters.label: Vaseline

parameters.help: Worn heads stand less proud of the drum and lose their grip on the tape. Black streaks trail bright edges first; then bands of snow and tearing drift through the picture and come and go, worst at the top and bottom, and the color gets noisy.
parameters.label: Head wear

parameters.help: Debris already on the heads when play starts. It holds them off the tape; each head carries its own, so one can be clogged while the other is clear — every other field fails. It shifts a little as the tape drags over it, so each head's picture drifts between worse and better.
parameters.label: Head dirt

parameters.help: How readily the heads collect what the tape sheds — low for a deck that's had a head-cleaning tape, high for one that never has. Every tape sheds a little, so an uncleaned deck clogs for a moment now and then on any tape; shedding tapes (mold, wear, flaws, sticky shed) clog it far more, and worn heads clog more easily. Clogs wipe off or knock loose.
parameters.label: Dirt buildup

parameters.help: How unevenly the two heads have aged: one reads a weaker signal than the other, and since they take turns, field by field, the picture flickers between them.
parameters.label: Head mismatch

parameters.help: How far the two heads are from exactly opposite on the drum, as a timing jump when the deck changes heads just before vertical sync. The bottom lines jump sideways and the TV's AFC chases the jump into the top of the next field — the bend called flagging.
parameters.label: Head switching

parameters.help: How hard the supply reel holds the tape back, against the deck that recorded it. Tighter stretches the tape, so each field's lines arrive a little later than the last, and the heads switch with a jump: skew, the top of the picture hooking sideways (further on a TV with a slow AFC response). Too slack and the tension wanders, so the top of the picture waves from side to side, and the tape stops hugging the heads where they meet it, so the top of the picture gets noisy. Up to half is a deck out of adjustment; past that is a stretched tape or a reel hardly braked at all, and the heads can no longer follow the tracks the whole way down (noise bars, worst on LP and EP).
parameters.label: Back tension

parameters.help: A tired transport: a worn drum motor and bearings, stretched belts, a lumpy pinch roller. The drum's speed wavers smoothly, so the picture's verticals bow and sway, in a shape that crawls and changes — broad bends on a TV with slow AFC, tighter ones on a fast one — and the tape's speed wavers, so the tracking breathes. The second half of the travel goes well past any deck still in use.
parameters.label: Flutter

parameters.help: The tracking control: it shifts when the tracking servo expects the control-track pulses, moving the tape along so the heads ride beside their tracks instead of on them (±100% is a whole track). The picture holds up until a head is mostly on its neighbor's track, recorded at the other azimuth — then noise bands break out wherever the tracks bend furthest from the heads' path. Tapes recorded on another deck need a little.
parameters.label: Tracking

parameters.help: Fast-forward picture search: the tape runs n× as fast, so each head's sweep crosses n−1 tracks. On the tracks of its own azimuth it reads picture; on the others, noise, with the color gone where the comb filter cancels it. The bars stand still at odd speeds and drift between them.
parameters.label: Search

parameters.help: The deck watches the signal coming off the heads and, where it drops out, repeats the line before — its sync pulse too. On, a dropout is a spark and a short smear of the line above; off, it shows as the demodulator's black and white streaks, and one that lands on a sync pulse jogs the picture sideways.
parameters.label: Dropout compensation
